definition: Carl Gustav Jung (1875-1961) founded analytical psychology, positing a collective unconscious populated by archetypes, a process of psychic integration he called individuation, and a principle of meaningful acausal connection he named synchronicity. Against Freud's emphasis on repressed sexuality, Jung treated religious and mythic material as psychologically real and potentially healing.
pkd_relevance: Jung was among PKD's most durable intellectual influences, present decades before 2-3-74 and central afterward. PKD read Jung seriously from the 1950s, absorbed the archetypes and the collective unconscious into his sense of how fiction works, and used Jungian categories — the shadow, the anima, individuation, synchronicity — as ready tools for interpreting both his characters and his own experiences. When the pink light came, Jung was one of the first frameworks he reached for.
in_the_fiction: Jungian patterning runs through PKD's female characters (the dark-haired girl as anima figure), his doubles and shadow-selves, and his interest in projection and possession. Novels like Martian Time-Slip and Eye in the Sky externalize private psychic contents into shared worlds, dramatizing something close to Jung's collective unconscious. Jung's presence is more atmospheric than doctrinal — PKD borrows the vocabulary and the mythic seriousness rather than building strict Jungian allegories.
in_the_exegesis: Jung recurs throughout the Exegesis as PKD tests whether 2-3-74 was an archetypal irruption from the collective unconscious rather than external revelation. He invokes individuation, the Self, synchronicity, and the numinous, and weighs a Jungian psychological reading against Gnostic and information-theoretic ones. Jung offers PKD a way to take the experience seriously without conceding it was mere pathology, though PKD never rests there.
intellectual_background: Jung's own sources — Gnosticism, alchemy, Eastern religion, the I Ching, medieval mysticism — overlap strikingly with PKD's later reading, which is part of why the fit felt natural to PKD. Jung's Answer to Job, his alchemical studies, and his commentary on the I Ching (with the Wilhelm translation PKD used) all feed directly into PKD's frameworks.
scholarly_debate: Scholars generally agree Jung is a major influence but differ on its depth and rigor. Some treat PKD as a genuinely Jungian writer whose late work enacts individuation; others note that PKD used Jung loosely and eclectically, one option among many he cycled through. There is also debate about whether the Jungian reading domesticates 2-3-74 too neatly, converting a disruptive event into a familiar psychological narrative PKD himself kept resisting.
